id_and_class.summary: Śaṅkara holds that pure, self-luminous consciousness is ultimate reality and that the true self (ātman) is numerically identical with Brahman. Consciousness reveals itself without needing a second awareness, so it is never an object, property, or product; the varied contents of experience belong to an insentient mind that consciousness illuminates. Ignorance makes this one consciousness appear as many embodied subjects, and liberation is the recognition that one has always been Brahman.

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness (cit) is self-luminous manifestation itself, the bare presence in which any content appears. It is the very nature (svarūpa) of the self and is identical with Brahman, the one nondual reality.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Mind is an insentient, subtle-material instrument (the internal organ, antaḥkaraṇa) whose states become experienced only through the consciousness that illuminates them. Body and mind are adjuncts that make the one consciousness appear limited and individual.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not applicable (Śaṅkara argues sentience cannot arise from what is intrinsically insentient)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Intentional structure belongs to the mind, while pure consciousness is non-intentional. The felt sense of being a particular subject is produced by superimposition (adhyāsa), the confusion of the witness with the body and mind it illuminates.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Colors, pains, emotions, and thoughts are modifications of the material internal organ, so qualitative character sits on the object side. Consciousness contributes only the fact that a content is manifest, and Śaṅkara offers no account of why a given experience has the specific character it has.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Brahman as nondual consciousness; ātman identical with Brahman; an insentient subtle-material mind; beginningless ignorance (avidyā); superimposition as the source of individual selves.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Consciousness is self-established and needs no means of knowledge to certify it, yet it is never known as an object. It is approached through Upaniṣadic teaching, reasoning (such as analysis of the three states), and contemplative assimilation.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Two standpoints. Empirically, consciousness functions as the passive witness (sākṣin) of an individual mind's states; ultimately, even the witness relation falls away, leaving one undivided consciousness. The individual self (jīva) is the witness apparently bounded by an adjunct, as space seems bounded by a pot.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal manifestation; self and self-knowledge; the illusion of individual ownership; deep sleep; liberation.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Self-luminosity (svaprakāśa) plus superimposition (adhyāsa). Consciousness manifests itself without a further awareness, and ignorance projects the properties of body and mind onto it, producing the ordinary ‘I’.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: Consciousness itself never changes or arises; only mental contents come and go. Individuality is an appearance that persists while ignorance lasts and is dissolved by knowledge, not by any change in consciousness.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Not located anywhere. Consciousness is single and unindividuated; it only appears localized when delimited by an individual mind and body.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: The witness is wholly passive and is unmodified by what it reveals. Its role is to make mental events experienced events, while all causal and qualitative work happens in the material mind.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Unity comes from the single invariant witness present across all changing contents, including waking, dreaming, and dreamless sleep.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Mental modifications (vṛttis) take the form of objects and represent them; consciousness illuminates these modifications and, through them, their objects. Later Advaita models of reflection and delimitation belong mostly to Śaṅkara's successors.
core_claims_and_evidence: If awareness needed a second awareness to be manifest, an infinite regress would follow, so consciousness must be self-luminous.
People report on waking that they slept well and knew nothing, which Śaṅkara takes to show that consciousness persisted without content in dreamless sleep.
Statements like ‘I am thin’ or ‘I am unhappy’ show that the witnessing self is routinely confused with body and mind.
Since sentience cannot originate in the insentient, consciousness must be the ontological primitive rather than a product of mind or matter.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical argument (regress and anti-emergence arguments), phenomenological analysis of the three states, and Upaniṣadic scripture.

empirics_and_critiques.known_empirical_interventions_or_tests: The deep-sleep argument has been compared with contemporary sleep science, notably by Evan Thompson, where evidence of minimal experience during deep sleep fits weaker readings as well.
empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Critics note that a memory-based deep-sleep argument cannot rule out after-the-fact reconstruction. How a beginningless ignorance relates to an awareness that is supposedly never modified is a long-standing difficulty. Vaidya argues that declaring consciousness fundamental does not solve the modern hard problem of why a particular subject experiences red rather than blue.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Śaṅkara supplies no psychophysical account connecting universal consciousness to the specific character of an individual's experience. The claim that consciousness is numerically one rests partly on scriptural authority, which limits evaluation by naturalistic standards.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Internally tight, since attributeless Brahman and liberation-as-recognition follow from the self-luminosity thesis. It directly opposes Buddhist no-self views, such as Nāgārjuna's, and reverses the explanatory direction of physicalism.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Śaṅkara does not address machines. Since minds of any kind are insentient instruments that consciousness illuminates, the question becomes whether a machine could serve as such an adjunct, which the view leaves open.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Consciousness is never produced by body or mind and does not change, so the death of the body does not touch it; what ends is only a misidentification.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: The whole analysis aims at liberation (mokṣa), the recognition that one's self is Brahman, the ground of all reality.

virtual_immortality.rationale: Copying a mind would copy only an insentient instrument and its contents. The conscious self is already unborn and undying, so digital continuation adds nothing to it.
